In this lab, you will build your own nonstationary model of extreme daily rainfall at Houston Hobby Airport and decide whether the evidence supports a published claim that it is rising.
Everyone uses the same record, and each of you makes different choices along the way.
On Wednesday, October 7, you will present your results in class and defend those choices, as practice for the oral exam.

## Objectives

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

1. Build a nonstationary extreme value model, choosing annual maxima or peaks over threshold, a covariate, and the form of the trend.
1. Report a change in the 100-year rainfall with an interval, and say what the interval leaves out.
1. Defend each choice behind your result.

### Rainfall data

You will analyze daily precipitation at Houston Hobby Airport, station `USW00012918` in NOAA's Global Historical Climatology Network, which is the record from Monday's lectures.
The file `hobby-daily.csv` has one row for each day with a valid reading, in millimeters.

@fig-daily plots every wet day.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-daily
#| fig-cap: "Daily rainfall at Houston Hobby Airport, wet days only."
daily = CSV.read(joinpath(here, "hobby-daily.csv"), DataFrame)
daily.year = year.(daily.date)
wet = filter(r -> r.prcp_mm > 0, daily)

fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{date}", ylabel=L"\text{daily rainfall (mm)}")
scatter!(ax, wet.date, wet.prcp_mm; color=colors[1], markersize=3)
fig
```

Not every year is complete.
@fig-days-per-year counts the days with a valid reading in each year.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-days-per-year
#| fig-cap: "Days with a valid reading in each year at Houston Hobby Airport."
days_per_year = combine(groupby(daily, :year), nrow => :n_days)
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 300))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel=L"\text{year}", ylabel=L"\text{days with a valid reading}")
scatterlines!(ax, days_per_year.year, days_per_year.n_days; color=colors[1], markersize=5)
fig
```

Many years are missing days, and 2026 is not over yet, so you need to decide how to handle the gaps.
Assume the data are *missing at random*: whether a day was recorded has nothing to do with how much rain fell.
To see when this might fail, picture a rain gauge that breaks in the heaviest storms.
A simple approach is to keep only the years with at least some number of valid days, such as 350.
You are welcome to try other cutoffs or other ways to filter.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
keep = days_per_year.year[(days_per_year.n_days .>= 350) .& (days_per_year.year .<= 2025)]
filter!(r -> r.year in keep, daily)
```

### Covariates

The file `covariates.csv` has three candidate covariates, one row per year from 1880 to 2025:

| Column | What it is | Source |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `log_CO2` | Natural log of annual mean atmospheric CO2, in parts per million | Before 1959, the Law Dome ice core record [@etheridge_lawdomeco2:1996; @macfarlingmeure_lawdomeextended:2006]; from 1959, the Mauna Loa annual means from NOAA's Global Monitoring Laboratory |
| `gmst` | Global mean surface temperature anomaly, in °C relative to 1951-1980 | NASA's GISTEMP version 4, January to December mean |
| `nino34` | Sea surface temperature anomaly in the Niño 3.4 region of the tropical Pacific, in °C relative to 1981-2010 | HadISST, from NOAA's Physical Sciences Laboratory, mean of the 12 calendar months |

CO2 and global temperature both rise over the record, so they are candidates for a long-term trend.
Niño 3.4 measures the El Niño-Southern Oscillation, which shifts from year to year with no long-term trend, so it is a candidate for explaining which years are wet.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-covariates
#| fig-cap: "The three candidate covariates over the years of the Hobby record."
covariates = filter(r -> r.year >= 1930, CSV.read(joinpath(here, "covariates.csv"), DataFrame))
fig = Figure(; size=(700, 500))
for (k, (col, label)) in enumerate(((:log_CO2, "log CO2"), (:gmst, "GMST anomaly (°C)"), (:nino34, "Niño 3.4 anomaly (°C)")))
    lines!(Axis(fig[k, 1]; ylabel=label, xlabel=k == 3 ? "year" : ""), covariates.year, covariates[!, col]; color=colors[k])
end
fig
```

## Your Challenge

@fagnant_spatiotemporal:2020 analyzed more than 600 rain gauges in southeast Texas and reported that the 100-year daily rainfall at Hobby rose by 1.93 mm per year (95% interval 1.50 to 2.35), with several methodological caveats.
In this lab, you will analyze a similar dataset and fit your own model.
You will make key choices, including whether to fit a Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) or Generalized Pareto Distribution (GPD) model, what covariates if any to use (and their functional form), and any priors to include.

Prepare a 5-10 minute slide presentation for class on Wednesday, October 7, that leads with your results and then explains your modeling choices.
**Key questions to answer are:**

1. What is your best estimate for the 10- and 100-year return levels in 2026?
1. How uncertain are these estimates?
1. How have these return levels changed over the past 40 years?
1. How will these return levels change over the next 40 years, and what assumptions do you make in projecting these?

Explain why you made each choice, as well as what it was.
**Key decisions to explain include:**

1. Did you fit a GEV to annual maxima or GPD to peaks over threshold?
   1. If GEV:
      1. How did you handle years with missing data?
   1. If GPD:
      1. How did you decluster?
      1. How did you select the threshold?
1. How did you decide whether to fit a nonstationary or stationary model?
   1. If nonstationary:
      1. How did you choose the covariates?
      1. How did you choose the functional form?
   1. If stationary:
      1. What gave you confidence in this choice?
1. How do you characterize uncertainty?
   1. If Bayesian: how did you choose priors?
   1. If bootstrap: how did you choose how to resample?

## My analysis

*I fit GEV models to the annual maximum daily rainfall at Hobby and compare a stationary model with nonstationary models that change with CO2. Each decision is stated with its reason as it comes up, and the four key questions are answered under Results.*

### Data

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
annmax = combine(groupby(daily, :year), :prcp_mm => maximum => :y)
annmax = sort(innerjoin(annmax, covariates; on=:year), :year)

# Print a table without the column types, row numbers, or size line
showtable(df) = show(df; eltypes=false, summary=false, show_row_number=false)

# "median [2.5%, 97.5%]" of a vector of draws
function fmt(v; digits=0)
    f = Printf.Format("%.$(digits)f [%.$(digits)f, %.$(digits)f]")
    return Printf.format(f, median(v), quantile(v, 0.025), quantile(v, 0.975))
end
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
@printf("%d complete years, %d to %d\n", nrow(annmax), minimum(annmax.year), maximum(annmax.year))
println(filter(r -> 200 <= r.n_days < 350, days_per_year))
```

**Decision: GEV on annual maxima**
*One value per year needs no threshold or declustering rule, and 80 complete years is enough to fit a few parameters.*

**Decision: keep years with at least 350 valid days.**
*I assume the data are missing at random. Before 1947, every year except 1940 and 1941 has under 60% of its days, so its maximum could be too low, and 2026 is not over. The only year near the cutoff is 1990 (334 days), so the exact cutoff barely matters.*

### Stationary or not, and which covariate

```{julia}
#| solution: false
candidates = [
    (name="M0 stationary", loc=Symbol[], sc=Symbol[]),
    (name="M1 μ ~ log CO2", loc=[:log_CO2], sc=Symbol[]),
    (name="M2 μ, log σ ~ log CO2", loc=[:log_CO2], sc=[:log_CO2]),
    (name="M3 μ, log σ ~ GMST", loc=[:gmst], sc=[:gmst]),
    (name="M4 μ ~ Niño 3.4", loc=[:nino34], sc=Symbol[]),
]
mle_fits = [gevfit(annmax, :y; locationcovid=c.loc, logscalecovid=c.sc) for c in candidates]
ll0 = loglike(mle_fits[1])
showtable(DataFrame(map(zip(candidates, mle_fits)) do (c, f)
    k = 3 + length(c.loc) + length(c.sc)
    lr = 2 * (loglike(f) - ll0)
    (model=c.name, AIC=round(2k - 2loglike(f); digits=1),
        p_vs_M0=k == 3 ? "" : @sprintf("%.2f", ccdf(Chisq(k - 3), lr)),
        ξ=round(params(f).β_shape[1]; digits=2))
end))
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
@printf("correlation of log CO2 and GMST: %.2f\n", cor(annmax.log_CO2, annmax.gmst))
```

**Decision: fit a trend model, but report its range rather than claim a trend.**
*No long-term covariate beats the stationary model: the CO2 and GMST models have p-values of 0.22 to 0.45 and a higher AIC than M0. That does not mean nothing changed, only that 80 years cannot show it clearly. I still fit a trend because the question is how much the 100-year level changed, and a stationary model answers zero by assumption.*

**Decision: log CO2 as the covariate.**
*It is a physical driver, and its future can be written as a scenario. GMST fits about the same, since it is almost the same signal (correlation 0.96). Niño 3.4 is the only significant covariate (p = 0.02), but it has no long-term trend and cannot be known for 2066, so it does not help with the questions.*

**Decision: location and log scale both linear in log CO2 (M2).**
*A location-only trend (M1) raises every return level by the same amount.Letting the scale change too allows the 100-year level to rise faster than a typical year, which is what Fagnant's claim is about.*
*The choice matters. M1 gives a 40-year change of +6 mm in the 100-year level and M2 gives +99 mm (@fig-forest).*

```{julia}
#| solution: false
early = filter(r -> r.year <= 1985, annmax)
recent = filter(r -> r.year >= 1986, annmax)
shift_mm = 1.93 * (mean(recent.year) - mean(early.year))

# Permutation test: how often does a random split of the same values give a gap this big?
perm_rng = MersenneTwister(2026)
function perm_test(a, b, stat; n_perm=20_000)
    observed = stat(b) - stat(a)
    pooled = vcat(a, b)
    n = length(a)
    hits = count(1:n_perm) do _
        p = shuffle(perm_rng, pooled)
        abs(stat(p[(n + 1):end]) - stat(p[1:n])) >= abs(observed)
    end
    return observed, hits / n_perm
end
for (name, stat) in (("median", median), ("mean", mean))
    gap, pval = perm_test(early.y, recent.y, stat)
    @printf("recent minus early, %-7s %+4.0f mm (permutation p = %.2f)\n", name * ":", gap, pval)
end
@printf("uniform shift at Fagnant's rate: %.0f mm\n", shift_mm)
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-halves
#| fig-cap: "Annual maxima of 1940-1985 (blue) and 1986-2025 (orange), each sorted and plotted at its return period within that half. The dashed line is the early half raised by 79 mm, where the recent half would sit if the whole distribution had shifted at Fagnant's rate."
plot_pos(n) = 1 ./ (1 .- (1:n) ./ (n + 1))   # Weibull plotting positions
fig = Figure(; size=(750, 420))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale=log10, xlabel="return period within each half (years)", ylabel="annual maximum (mm)",
    xticks=([1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 40], ["1", "2", "5", "10", "20", "40"]))
lines!(ax, plot_pos(nrow(early)), sort(early.y) .+ shift_mm; color=:gray50, linestyle=:dash, linewidth=2,
    label=@sprintf("1940-1985 + %.0f mm", shift_mm))
scatterlines!(ax, plot_pos(nrow(early)), sort(early.y); color=colors[1], markersize=7, label="1940-1985")
scatterlines!(ax, plot_pos(nrow(recent)), sort(recent.y); color=colors[2], markersize=7, label="1986-2025")
text!(ax, plot_pos(nrow(recent))[end], maximum(recent.y); text="Harvey", align=(:right, :bottom), offset=(-6, 2), fontsize=12)
axislegend(ax; position=:lt, framevisible=false)
fig
```

*@fig-halves compares the two halves of the record directly from the data, without fitting a GEV. The recent 40 years are a little wetter (median +21 mm), but random splits of the same data give a gap this large 13% of the time, so this could be chance. If Fagnant's rise came from shifting the whole distribution (location only), the recent half would sit 79 mm higher, on the dashed line. It does not, so a location-only change of this magnitude is not supported by the observed data. If the 100-year level did rise that much, most of the rise must come from a wider tail (scale), which is why M2 lets the scale change too.*

### Fitting the models

**Decision: Bayesian fits with flat priors on the trend.**
I keep the package defaults (flat priors on the coefficients, ξ uniform on -0.5 to 0.5) so the data set the trend, rather than an assumption about how fast extremes should grow.
As a check, I refit M2 with a prior based on Clausius-Clapeyron scaling. About 7% more moisture per °C of warming, converted to log CO2 through the observed GMST-CO2 relationship, with the prior standard deviation at twice that rate.
I also refit M2 without 2017 to see how much Harvey drives the result.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| output: false
fit_m0 = gevfitbayes(annmax, :y; rng=rng, progress=false)
fit_m1 = gevfitbayes(annmax, :y; locationcovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)
fit_m2 = gevfitbayes(annmax, :y; locationcovid=[:log_CO2], logscalecovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)

# Prior scaled by Clausius-Clapeyron (about 7% more moisture per °C of warming):
# convert to a change per unit of log CO2 with the observed GMST-log CO2 slope,
# and set the prior sd to twice that rate, centered on no trend.
cc = 0.07
gmst_per_logco2 = cov(annmax.gmst, annmax.log_CO2) / var(annmax.log_CO2)
sd_x = std(annmax.log_CO2)   # the package works per sd of the covariate
μ_ref = params(mle_fits[1]).β_location[1]
cc_prior = (location=Normal(0, 2cc * gmst_per_logco2 * μ_ref * sd_x),
    logscale=Normal(0, 2cc * gmst_per_logco2 * sd_x))
fit_m2cc = gevfitbayes(annmax, :y; locationcovid=[:log_CO2], logscalecovid=[:log_CO2],
    trend_priors=cc_prior, rng=rng, progress=false)

# Same as M2 without 2017 (Harvey), to see how much one storm matters
fit_m2_noharvey = gevfitbayes(filter(r -> r.year != 2017, annmax), :y;
    locationcovid=[:log_CO2], logscalecovid=[:log_CO2], rng=rng, progress=false)
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
fits = [("M0", fit_m0), ("M1", fit_m1), ("M2", fit_m2), ("M2, CC prior", fit_m2cc), ("M2, no Harvey", fit_m2_noharvey)]
showtable(DataFrame(map(fits) do (name, f)
    st = DataFrame(summarystats(f.estimate))
    (model=name, max_rhat=round(maximum(st.rhat); digits=3), min_ess=round(Int, minimum(st.ess_bulk)),
        ξ=fmt(params(f).β_shape[:, 1]; digits=2))
end))
```

All chains converged (rhat at most 1.004, effective sample size above 1,200).
The shape ξ is about 0.15 to 0.20, a heavy upper tail, and it stays well inside its -0.5 to 0.5 prior, so that prior does not constrain it.

### Results

CO2 for 2026 and 2066 is extended from the 2015-2025 growth rate, because the covariate file ends in 2025.

```{julia}
#| solution: false
ppm = exp.(covariates.log_CO2)
co2_rate = (ppm[end] - ppm[end-10]) / 10   # ppm per year, 2015 to 2025
log_co2_obs(yr) = covariates.log_CO2[findfirst(==(yr), covariates.year)]
co2_path(yr, r) = yr <= 2025 ? log_co2_obs(yr) : log(ppm[end] + co2_rate + r * (yr - 2026))

key_years = [1986, 2026, 2066]
x_key = co2_path.(key_years, co2_rate)
@printf("CO2: %.0f ppm in 1986, %.0f in 2026, %.0f in 2066 (+%.1f ppm per year)\n", exp.(x_key)..., co2_rate)

# Return-level draws (rows) at log CO2 values xs (columns)
function rl_draws(fit, T, xs; trend=true)
    trend || return repeat(returnlevel(fit, T), 1, length(xs))
    return returnlevel(fit, T; locationcov=[xs], logscalecov=[xs])
end
function rl_draws_m1(fit, T, xs)
    return returnlevel(fit, T; locationcov=[xs])
end
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
answer_models = [
    ("M2 (main)", T -> rl_draws(fit_m2, T, x_key)),
    ("M2, CC prior", T -> rl_draws(fit_m2cc, T, x_key)),
    ("M1", T -> rl_draws_m1(fit_m1, T, x_key)),
    ("M0 stationary", T -> rl_draws(fit_m0, T, x_key; trend=false)),
]
showtable(DataFrame(vec([begin
    r = g(T)
    (model=name, T=T, level_2026=fmt(r[:, 2]),
        change_1986_2026=fmt(r[:, 2] .- r[:, 1]), change_2026_2066=fmt(r[:, 3] .- r[:, 2]))
end for (name, g) in answer_models, T in (10, 100)])))
```

```{julia}
#| solution: false
r100 = rl_draws(fit_m2, 100, x_key)
@printf("M2: chance the 100-year level rose since 1986 = %.2f; chance it rose at least 77 mm = %.2f\n",
    mean(r100[:, 2] .> r100[:, 1]), mean(r100[:, 2] .- r100[:, 1] .>= 77))
r100h = rl_draws(fit_m2_noharvey, 100, x_key)
@printf("M2 without Harvey: 100-year change since 1986 = %s mm\n", fmt(r100h[:, 2] .- r100h[:, 1]))
```

**Q1. 2026 return levels.**
*From M2, the 2026 10-year daily rainfall is 235 mm and the 100-year is 429 mm (@fig-rl-time).*

**Q2. Uncertainty.**
*The 95% intervals are 175 to 333 mm and 285 to 742 mm.*
*The 100-year interval is wide because the tail is heavy and 80 years say little about a 1-in-100 event.*
*The model choice matters as much: the CC prior gives 199 and 360 mm, and the stationary model 191 and 353 mm.*
*The intervals leave out errors at the gauge and the chance that the CO2 relationship is wrong.*

**Q3. Change over the past 40 years.**
*M2 says the 100-year level rose 99 mm since 1986 (-25 to +311), about 2.5 mm per year.*
*That is close to Fagnant's 1.93 mm per year but much less certain, and the chance it rose at all is 0.93.*
*The 10-year level rose 49 mm (-9 to +132).*
*The answer depends on the model (@fig-forest): a location-only trend gives +6 mm, the CC prior +15 mm, and dropping Harvey alone cuts the M2 change to +67 mm. So the data are consistent with both no change and Fagnant's estimate.*

**Q4. Change over the next 40 years.**
*I assume CO2 keeps rising at the 2015-2025 rate, from 430 ppm in 2026 to 535 ppm in 2066, and that the fitted relationship holds beyond the CO2 levels in the record.*
*Under M2, the 100-year level rises another 137 mm (-23 to +617) and the 10-year level 63 mm (-8 to +250).*
*The upper end of that range is very wide because it extends a scale trend that the data barely constrain.*
*The CC prior gives a much smaller +17 mm (-37 to +104), but it holds only if extreme rainfall follows Clausius-Clapeyron scaling, which this record cannot confirm, so I keep the flat-prior result as the main answer.*
*If CO2 stops rising, the levels stop changing (@fig-projection).*


```{julia}
#| solution: false
#| label: fig-projection
#| fig-cap: "100-year daily rainfall to 2066 under three CO2 paths: CO2 stops rising after 2026 (blue), the 2015-2025 growth continues (orange), and growth speeds up by half (green). Left: M2 with flat priors. Right: M2 with the CC prior. Lines are posterior medians and shading 95% intervals."
scenarios = [0.0, co2_rate, 1.5co2_rate]
hist_years = collect(minimum(annmax.year):2025)
fut_years = collect(2025:2066)
fig = Figure(; size=(850, 380))
proj_axes = Axis[]
for (j, (title, f)) in enumerate((("M2, flat priors", fit_m2), ("M2, CC prior", fit_m2cc)))
    ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; title=title, xlabel="year", ylabel=j == 1 ? "100-year daily rainfall (mm)" : "")
    push!(proj_axes, ax)
    r = rl_draws(f, 100, co2_path.(hist_years, co2_rate))
    band!(ax, hist_years, quantile.(eachcol(r), 0.025), quantile.(eachcol(r), 0.975); color=(:gray50, 0.25))
    lines!(ax, hist_years, median.(eachcol(r)); color=:black, linewidth=2)
    for (k, rate) in enumerate(scenarios)
        r = rl_draws(f, 100, co2_path.(fut_years, rate))
        band!(ax, fut_years, quantile.(eachcol(r), 0.025), quantile.(eachcol(r), 0.975); color=(colors[k], 0.15))
        lines!(ax, fut_years, median.(eachcol(r)); color=colors[k], linewidth=2.5)
    end
end
linkyaxes!(proj_axes...)
fig
```

**Bottom line.**
**Best estimate in 2026:**

*$𝑧_10$ (2026)=235[175,333], $𝑧_100$ (2026)=429[285,742]  mm/day*

**Uncertainty:** *Large. The 100-year interval spans 285–742 mm. Across the models, posterior median estimates of the 40-year change range from +6 to +99 mm. Under the main M2 model, the 95% credible interval is [-25, 311] mm.*

**Past 40 years:** *the main model suggests an increase, especially in the upper tail, but the 95% credible interval for the change includes zero.*

**Next 40 years:** *under continued CO2 growth, return levels likely rise further; this is a projection under assumptions instead of a guaranteed forecast.*

*Hence, Hobby rainfall extremes may be increasing, but one gauge alone cannot pin down the 100-year tail with high confidence.*
